title: Trump admin nearly wipes out National Council on the Humanities
description_short: Trump admin nearly wipes out National Council on the Humanities
description_medium: On October 1, 2025, the White House terminated most members of the National Council on the Humanities, leaving four, all appointed by Trump. The White House said Trump wanted members whose views aligned more closely with his own. Because the council needs 14 members for a quorum, the dismissals left it unable to function pending new Senate-confirmed appointments.
description_long: The White House terminated most members of the National Council on the Humanities on October 1, 2025, leaving four members, all appointed by President Donald Trump. The administration said Trump hoped to appoint people whose views aligned more closely with his vision, and offered no further explanation in the account. The council advises the National Endowment for the Humanities, which supports museums, historic sites, schools, libraries, public media, research, and humanities councils across the states and territories. The council requires 14 members for a quorum, so reducing its membership to four left it unable to conduct its regular work until new members could be appointed and confirmed by the Senate. The episode changed the composition of a federal advisory body and interrupted its ability to advise the endowment. The supplied report records the administration’s stated rationale and the quorum requirement; it does not establish the views of the dismissed members or describe a specific grant or program lost because of the vacancies.

preserved_fields.title: Trump admin nearly wipes out National Council on the Humanities
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump admin nearly wipes out National Council on the Humanities

title: Trump suspends green card lottery program for 50,000 recipients due to one criminal
description_short: Trump suspends green card lottery program for 50,000 recipients due to one criminal
description_medium: On December 18, 2025, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced that she was suspending the diversity immigrant visa lottery at Trump’s direction after Portuguese national Claudio Neves Valente was identified as the suspect in shootings at Brown University and the killing of an MIT professor. The program makes up to 50,000 visas available annually. The supplied account does not establish the suspension’s formal scope or effect on pending applicants.
description_long: Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced on December 18, 2025, that she had been directed by President Donald Trump to suspend the diversity immigrant visa lottery. The announcement followed the identification of Portuguese national Claudio Neves Valente as the suspect in shootings at Brown University and the killing of an MIT professor. The account says Valente entered the United States on a student visa in 2000 and received a diversity visa in 2017. The annual program makes up to 50,000 visas available to people from countries with lower rates of immigration to the United States. In the 2025 lottery, nearly 20 million people applied and more than 131,000 were selected when spouses were included; selection did not itself grant permanent residence, which required screening and an interview. The reports supplied here do not include the formal suspension notice, specify how long the pause would last, or explain how current applicants and selectees would be treated. The event is an announced program suspension tied to one suspect’s case; the available evidence does not establish its final implementation or impact.

preserved_fields.title: Trump suspends green card lottery program for 50,000 recipients due to one criminal
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump suspends green card lottery program for 50,000 recipients due to one criminal

notes: Needs context: source notes support Noem’s announcement and the suspect’s visa history, but not the formal suspension notice, duration, or effects on current applicants. The title calls the suspect a “criminal”; no conviction is supplied.
proposed_correction: Describe Valente as a suspect and the program action as an announced suspension; add the notice’s terms and applicant effects when documented.

title: Trump FBI raids home of Washington Post reporter
description_short: Trump FBI raids home of Washington Post reporter
description_medium: On January 14, 2026, the FBI executed a search warrant at Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson’s Virginia home. Agents told her she was not the target of a criminal investigation and said they were seeking information about Maryland system administrator Aurelio Perez-Lugones, who was suspected of mishandling classified material. Investigators searched Natanson’s phone, laptops, and watch.
description_long: The FBI executed a search warrant at Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson’s Virginia home on the morning of January 14, 2026. Agents told Natanson that she was not herself the subject of a criminal investigation and said they were seeking information about Maryland system administrator Aurelio Perez-Lugones. Court records cited in the supplied account said Perez-Lugones was suspected of mishandling classified information related to an unspecified country; reports said classified intelligence documents were found at his home. Agents searched Natanson’s phone, personal laptop, a Washington Post-issued laptop, and Garmin watch. The search raised press-freedom concerns because investigators sought material from a journalist who was not accused of a crime. The account notes that Attorney General Pam Bondi had removed a prior Justice Department policy limiting searches of reporters’ records, while the Privacy Protection Act continued to protect journalistic work materials in many circumstances. The packet does not include the warrant or establish whether its execution violated that law, what information was recovered, or whether charges followed. It also does not show that Trump personally directed the search.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump FBI raids home of Washington Post reporter

notes: Needs context: the supplied account documents the search and the stated target of the investigation, but does not include the warrant, inventory, results, or legal disposition. It does not establish that Trump personally directed the search.

title: Trump: Brooks and Capehart on Trump's loyalty demands
description_short: Trump: Brooks and Capehart on Trump's loyalty demands
description_medium: On May 22, 2026, David Brooks and Jonathan Capehart joined PBS host William Brangham to discuss Trump’s influence over Republican primaries, a departing Cabinet member, and Democrats’ election-loss analysis. The transcript cites Trump’s calls to defeat Republicans Thomas Massie and Bill Cassidy, his support for Indiana redistricting allies, and his endorsement of Ken Paxton over Senator John Cornyn.
description_long: PBS NewsHour’s May 22, 2026, Politics Monday segment brought together David Brooks of The Atlantic, Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW, and host William Brangham. They discussed Trump’s influence over Republican primaries, another Cabinet departure, and Democrats’ analysis of their prior election loss. In the transcript, Brangham pointed to Trump’s efforts to unseat Representatives Thomas Massie and Senator Bill Cassidy after they opposed him, and to local Indiana legislators who resisted his redistricting preferences. Capehart described the pressure facing Texas Senator John Cornyn after Trump endorsed Ken Paxton in the Republican Senate primary. Brooks said Trump had worked to make the party a MAGA party, even at the potential cost of short-term electoral losses. The segment was political analysis, not a formal finding about election rules or misconduct. Its discussion concerned how Trump’s primary influence could shape lawmakers’ incentives and party identity. The episode summary and transcript identify the panelists and examples but do not quantify how many voters or officials changed positions as a result.

title: Administration Officials Caught in Self-Dealing Contract Scandal
description_short: Administration Officials Caught in Self-Dealing Contract Scandal
description_medium: During May 2026, the administration faced intense scrutiny over allegations of blatant self-dealing and corruption. Reports revealed that government contracts were being awarded to corporations in which senior administration officials held direct financial interests. Additionally, there were highly questionable funding allocations for transportation-related 'reality show' projects, further cementing the administration's reputation as a grift to funnel taxpayer money to loyalists.
description_long: NBC News reported that George Zoley, founder of private-prison contractor GEO Group, said Corey Lewandowski sought compensation for helping protect or grow the company’s federal contracts. At the time, Lewandowski was an unpaid special government employee advising Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and was described by sources as influential in contract decisions. Zoley reportedly rejected the request during the 2024 transition. In a later meeting in early 2025, Zoley offered a consulting retainer, but sources said Lewandowski wanted payment tied to new or renewed Department of Homeland Security contracts; Zoley declined. The report said two GEO contracts were later shortened and some facilities stood idle. A DHS official told NBC that Lewandowski then advised against awarding more contracts to GEO, while the company believed the contract changes were connected to its refusal. These are reported accounts from sources, not an adjudicated finding of bribery or a proven cause for the contract decisions. The supplied article does not support the existing medium’s separate reference to transportation reality-show funding or a general claim that contracts went to firms in which officials held direct financial interests.
